questions.question: If A has shape (2, 3) and B has shape (3, 2), what shape does A @ B have?
questions.explanation: The inner dimensions 3 and 3 agree, and the outer dimensions remain: two rows from A and two columns from B.

questions.question: What is the element-wise product of [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and [[5, 6], [7, 8]]?
questions.explanation: Multiply entries at matching positions: 1*5, 2*6, 3*7, and 4*8. Matrix multiplication would sum products instead.

questions.question: For A = [[4, 7], [2, 6]], what are det(A) and A inverse?
options: det(A)=0, so every 2x2 matrix is singular
questions.explanation: The determinant is 4*6 - 7*2 = 10. The inverse is (1/10)[[6,-7],[-2,4]], which is the displayed decimal matrix.

questions.question: How does the Matrix class add a bias of shape (1, 3) to an output of shape (2, 3)?
options: It repeats the output row to make a (1, 3) matrix
It adds the bias row to each output row
It multiplies the two matrices element by element
It rejects the shapes because they are not identical
questions.explanation: The implementation explicitly broadcasts a one-row bias across the two output rows, matching the common dense-layer operation.

questions.question: In a dense layer with W shape (4, 3), x shape (3, 1), and b shape (4, 1), what is the shape after relu(W @ x + b)?
questions.explanation: W @ x produces (4,1), b has the same shape, and ReLU changes values but not shape.

questions.question: The Matrix class raises an inner-dimensions error for (2, 3) @ (2, 1). What is the direct fix?
options: Add the matrices element by element instead
Change the output shape label without changing either matrix
Take the determinant of the rectangular operands
Use a right operand with shape (3, n), or transpose it if that matches the data
questions.explanation: The left matrix has three columns, so the right matrix must have three rows. A transpose is appropriate only when it produces that compatible orientation.
